items.title: Fine for manufacturing company after man left as ‘a shadow of his former self’
items.summary: Gary Taylor, suffered multiple injuries when he was hit on the head by a one- tonne metal hopper He spent three weeks in hospital and had to take seven months off work E H Hassell & Sons Limited fined £300,000 for failing to properly plan for work A Staffordshire-based manufacturing company has been fined £300,000 […]
items.body:
- Gary Taylor, suffered multiple injuries when he was hit on the head by a one- tonne metal hopper
- He spent three weeks in hospital and had to take seven months off work
- E H Hassell & Sons Limited fined £300,000 for failing to properly plan for work
A Staffordshire-based manufacturing company has been fined £300,000 after a family man was left with injuries so serious he became ‘a shadow of his former self’.
Gary Taylor, who was 63 at the time, spent three weeks in hospital and needed seven months off work, following the incident on 24 March 2025.
The grandfather had been working for E H Hassell & Sons Limited at its site on Newstead Ind Estate in Trentham. He was one of several workers involved in the unloading of a lorry trailer containing various steel components for a large filtration system.
The workers had improvised a system to unload the metal hopper with a forklift truck, placing the forks underneath the unsecured load to lift it from the trailer bed. However, as it slid from the forks, it struck Mr Taylor in the head as he was stood alongside it. His injuries included fractures to his skull, neck and spine, two broken ribs and a severe laceration to his forehead which required 17 staples and 14 stitches.
Mr Taylor described how the incident has had a lasting impact on his life.
“During my time off recuperating from my injuries, the seven months I was off work, I had no interest in anything,” he said.
“I know my wife thinks that I won’t be around with her in my eighties, she has constant worry that something is going to happen to me.
“She never thought like that before my accident.
“For me, I have no idea what the future holds.
“I can only hope that I will get better as time goes on and I become more like the old man I used to be – a supportive husband, father and grandfather to my grandchildren.
“I want to be a person that hopefully will become more of a person than a shadow of my former self.”
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the lifting operation had not been properly planned by a competent person. The characteristics of the load, including its weight, size, centre of gravity and lifting points, had not been adequately assessed, and no safe system of work had been put in place.
Moving an object of this size and weight was not a regular task at the site and there was no established system of work for it.
HSE guidance on Planning and organising lifting operations – HSE states that it is important to properly resource, plan and organise lifting operations so they are carried out in a safe manner.
E H Hassell & Sons Limited of Alderflat Drive, Trentham, Staffordshire pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 8(1) of the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 and were fined £300,000 and ordered to pay costs of £5,690 at a hearing at Birmingham Magistrates’ Court on 23 October 2026.
HSE inspector Claire Whitehurst said:
“The failures here resulted in an experienced worker suffering life-changing injuries.
“The company failed to properly plan the lifting operation or implement a safe system of work.
“Mr Taylor suffered serious injuries which could easily have resulted in his death. He has been left with facial scarring, and both he and his family have been deeply affected by this traumatic experience.
“Employers must ensure that lifting operations are properly planned by a competent person and carried out safely. This is especially important for non-routine tasks involving heavy or awkward loads.”
The HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer, Julian White and supported by HSE paralegal officer, Stephen Grabe. The investigation was supported by visiting officer, Natalka Heath.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- Relevant guidance can be found here: Planning and organising lifting operations – HSE

items.title: Bed springs company fined after worker injured in warehouse collision
items.summary: CCTV captures moment a ride-on pallet truck collides with fork lift truck inside busy warehouse in Barnsley 20-year-old worker suffered several fractures to his foot and nerve damage Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited had failed to consider impact of changes it had made to workplace transport routes CCTV has captured the moment a young […]
items.body:
- CCTV captures moment a ride-on pallet truck collides with fork lift truck inside busy warehouse in Barnsley
- 20-year-old worker suffered several fractures to his foot and nerve damage
- Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited had failed to consider impact of changes it had made to workplace transport routes
CCTV has captured the moment a young worker was injured when the ride-on pallet truck he was using collided with a fork lift truck in a warehouse in Yorkshire.
Bed spring manufacturer Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited has been fined after Charlie O’Dowd was injured in the incident at its Long Royd warehouse in Barnsley on 14 November 2024.
The then 20-year-old had been using a ride-on pallet truck during the installation of new automated machinery within the warehouse. However, his truck, which was unguarded, collided with a fork lift truck being driven by another employee, resulting in multiple fractures to his foot, as well as longer term nerve damage.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the company had made changes to its workplace transport routes to accommodate the installation works taking place. However, these changes meant that both ride-on pallet trucks and fork lift trucks were required to use the same routes, within what was a busy stock loading area. Visibility was limited and vehicle movements had increased.
The HSE investigation concluded that the company had focused on the installation of the new machinery but had failed to adequately consider the impact that significant changes to workplace transport arrangements would have on worker safety. The changes to vehicle routes had not been properly risk assessed before being implemented.
Every year, there are accidents involving transport in the workplace, some of which result in people being killed. HSE guidance explains what should be done to keep workers safe – Introduction to workplace transport safety – HSE.
Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited, pleaded guilty to a breach of Section 2(1) of the Health & Safey at Work etc. Act 1974 in relation to the safe use of workplace transport within the warehouse. The company was fined £80,000 and ordered to pay full costs of £3,374 at Leeds Magistrates Court on 20 October 2026.
HSE Inspector Chris Parker said:
“This case highlights the importance of carefully assessing the wider safety implications of any changes made within a workplace, even where those changes may be temporary.
“When workplace transport routes are altered, employers must ensure that the risks created by those changes are properly assessed and controlled before they are introduced.
“Had suitable planning and risk assessment been carried out, this incident could have been prevented.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Julian White and paralegal officer Zara Salman and advocacy undertaken by enforcement lawyer Arfaq Nabi.

items.title: Half-a-million pound fine for company after worker suffers 40 per cent burns
items.summary: Three-tonne steel beam fell into bath of molten zinc that created wave that covered worker 33-year-old man spent 11 days in intensive care requiring 13 operations Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited fined more than £500k after HSE investigation finds chains used to lift beam were damaged and deteriorated One of Britain’s leading steel galvanizers has been […]
items.body:
- Three-tonne steel beam fell into bath of molten zinc that created wave that covered worker
- 33-year-old man spent 11 days in intensive care requiring 13 operations
- Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited fined more than £500k after HSE investigation finds chains used to lift beam were damaged and deteriorated
One of Britain’s leading steel galvanizers has been fined more than £500,000 after one of its workers suffered 40 per cent burns to his body when hit by a wave of molten zinc at its site in Devon.
The employee was working for Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited at its site in Marsh End, Lords Meadow Industrial Estate in Crediton, Mid Devon, when the incident happened on 12 October 2021.
Hot dip galvanizing is a process that provides long-term protection against rust and corrosion of steel products. On the day in question, a lifting chain, carrying a roller steel joist weighing nearly three tonnes, failed. The beam fell into a galvanizing bath and the resulting wave of molten zinc covered the 33-year-old, before hitting a wall and surging back along the floor towards him.
CCTV footage from the scene shows the worker alight and running towards the emergency shower where his clothes were removed and he was doused in water. He was initially treated at the scene by paramedics, before being taken by air ambulance to Southmead hospital in Bristol. He had suffered 40 per cent burns and remained in intensive care for 11 days undergoing 13 separate operations. Any remaining healthy skin was grafted to repair his burnt body.
During his lengthy treatment the man suffered infection and sepsis leaving him with multiple long-term health conditions.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the set of chains used to lift the heavy steel beam had signs of damage and deterioration and there was a failure to withdraw them. Crucially, the chains had not undergone their mandatory regular inspection.
The investigation also revealed that the load slinging arrangement used at the time of the incident was incorrect, which meant that the load being lifted was greater than the safe limit for the chains. The risk assessment in place at the time of the incident for “immersion & swilling” had no reference to checks on chains, or what type of sling configuration to use.
Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited failed to meet several regulations and standards. Under the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations (LOLER) 1998, lifting accessories must be thoroughly examined by a competent person at least every six months. Both the Lifting Equipment Engineers Association (LEEA) code of practice and the user manual for the chain manufacturer state that chain slings used in acidic environments, such as zinc galvanising, should be inspected before each day’s use.
The Health and Safety Executive publishes freely available guidance which underlines the importance of thorough inspection of lifting equipment, including the benefits of an ‘examination scheme’.
Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited of Stafford Street, Willenhall, West Midlands, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 3(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £566,666 and ordered to pay £15,521 in costs at Bristol Magistrates Court on Wednesday 14 October 2026.
HSE inspector Alexander Ashen said:
“This wholly-avoidable incident led to a young man having to endure truly terrible injuries – and the disturbing truth is that the consequences could have been even worse.
“It is shocking that an industry-leading firm,, with considerable resources at its disposal, should risk the lives of its workers with substandard inspection protocols.
“Our thoughts are with the victim at the heart of this incident, his friends and family, and all those at the site who have been affected by what happened that day.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Gemma Zakrzewski, Paralegal Officer, Farhat Basir and Rowena Goodwin, Enforcement Advocate.

items.title: Electrical wholesaler fined £4million after worker’s crush injuries mean he now needs 24/7 care
items.summary: 40-year-old father of one was crushed by load weighing over 200kg His injuries were so serious he now lives in a care home City Electrical Factors Limited failed to plan work properly and fined £4million A Telford-based electrical wholesaler and manufacturer has been fined £4million after an employee sustained life-changing injuries when he was crushed […]
items.body:
- 40-year-old father of one was crushed by load weighing over 200kg
- His injuries were so serious he now lives in a care home
- City Electrical Factors Limited failed to plan work properly and fined £4million
A Telford-based electrical wholesaler and manufacturer has been fined £4million after an employee sustained life-changing injuries when he was crushed during loading operations using a forklift truck.
The 40-year-old father of one from Telford was working for City Electrical Factors Limited at its Proteus Switchgear Industrial Division on 4 October 2024 when the incident happened.
The man had been acting as a “spotter” while a forklift truck loaded heavy switchboard equipment onto a flatbed lorry. The load, which weighed 231kg, was not secured to the forklift and fell on top of him. He sustained brain and spine injuries and underwent lifesaving surgery. However, he can no longer do anything for himself and is unable to communicate with others. As a result of these injuries, he now lives in a care home and requires 24/7 care.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that City Electrical Factors Limited failed to ensure that the lifting operation was properly planned by a competent person, appropriately supervised and carried out in a safe manner. There was no risk assessment or lift plan, and employees had not been provided with information or instructions about the lifting operation, despite this being a regular activity.
The investigation also found that the load could have been secured to the forklift truck using pre-existing anchor points. The load also had lifting eyes welded to it, which meant that the crane attached to the delivery lorry could have been used as a safer alternative to the forklift truck. Instead, employees were appointed as “spotters” and were expected to steady the loads whilst they were being moved and lifted. This was clearly an unsafe and unnecessary system of work.
HSE guidance states that lift plans should address the risks identified by the risk assessment and identify the resources required, the procedures and the responsibilities so that risks are managed, and any lifting operation is carried out safely. You can read more about our guidance here: Planning and organising lifting operations – HSE.
City Electrical Factors Limited pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £4m and ordered to pay £6,304 in costs at Birmingham Magistrates Court on 16 October 2026.
HSE inspector Keeley Eves said:
“This incident had truly tragic consequences.
“To make matters worse it was completely avoidable and caused by a failure to properly plan for the job taking place.
“The company could have used safer alternative methods to lift the load, such as the lorry-mounted crane which was available, instead of using the forklift truck.
“Instead, the employee was placed at unnecessary risk and now has to live with his devastating injuries.
“Loading and unloading operations remain one of the most hazardous transport activities in the workplace. Employers must ensure that lifting operations are properly planned by competent persons, supervised and carried out safely.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Julian White and paralegal officer Lynne Thomas, while the investigation was supported by visiting officer Sarah Ough.

items.title: Fishing fleet company fined following engine room fatality
items.summary: Apprentice engineer Conor Moseley, 20, died when a fire suppression system unexpectedly activated, filling the engine room with toxic gases. HSE investigation found no safe system of work existed for coordinating multiple contractors working in the cramped engine room, and no effective emergency plan was in place. Company fined after pleading guilty to two charges […]
items.body:
- Apprentice engineer Conor Moseley, 20, died when a fire suppression system unexpectedly activated, filling the engine room with toxic gases.
- HSE investigation found no safe system of work existed for coordinating multiple contractors working in the cramped engine room, and no effective emergency plan was in place.
- Company fined after pleading guilty to two charges under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.
One of Britain’s leading fishing industry firms has been fined £100,000 after an apprentice engineer died in the engine room of a trawler in Newlyn Harbour.
Conor Moseley, aged 20, died when fire extinguisher gases left him unable to escape the engine room of a trawler on 15 November 2019.
Conor and three other workers were carrying out work on the Resurgam, a fishing vessel owned and operated by W. Stevenson & Sons Limited, when a fire suppression system being installed by Ocean Engineering (Fire) Ltd unexpectedly activated. It filled the engine room with hot, toxic gases, creating dangerous conditions and making it difficult to see.
The small, enclosed engine room had only one way in and out. Workers had to climb a ladder and pass through a hatch one at a time, passing through a gas jet in excess of 75°C. The other workers managed to climb out, but Conor was overcome by carbon monoxide and other substances, leaving him unable to escape.
His colleagues tried to rescue him, putting themselves at risk in the process, but they were unable to reach him. Cornwall Fire and Rescue Service later rescued Conor from the engine room, but he could not be revived.
Tracy Moseley, Conor’s mother, reflected on her son’s life and the impact his death has had on them.
“Growing up Conor loved nothing better than helping out on his dad’s boat.
“Conor always made himself available to help his father when he came in from sea and would be ready to help him land his catch even after a full day’s work. Now for Steve, my husband, there is just an empty place that cannot be filled.
“All we have now are his ashes which are kept in his bedroom. Every morning I go in and say, ‘morning little man I love you’ and blow him a kiss. I never say ‘good morning’ as it can never be a good morning without him.
“At night I blow him a kiss and say ‘night night little man, I love you’.”
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the risks created by several contractors working in the cramped engine room had not been properly considered. One contractor described the room as a mess, with poor lighting and trip hazards, and said that at one point six or seven people were working in the space. One witness described it as chaos.
There was no safe system of work for installing the fire suppression system and no effective emergency plan. A permit-to-work system could have been used to coordinate the different activities and ensure they were carried out safely. HSE’s Safety in Docks Approved Code of Practice highlights the need for parties to work together and have an overall written plan covering responsibilities, shared risks and emergency arrangements.
At Truro Crown Court on 15 October 2026, W. Stevenson & Sons Ltd entered guilty pleas to two charges under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, sections 2(1) and 3(1). The company was fined £100,000 and ordered to pay full costs of £27,906.
HSE principal inspector Helena Allum said:
“This was a particularly complicated case requiring significant HSE specialist and scientific input. A number of duty holders played a part in the circumstances leading to the death of Conor; all were investigated.
“While W. Stevenson & Sons Ltd was not responsible for the fire suppression system going off unexpectedly, it was responsible for considering what could go wrong during the installation and maintenance activities, and coordinating them so that as few people as possible were put at risk.
“They had not considered how workers could be quickly rescued in an emergency and receive prompt medical attention. This should be a key consideration when people are working in a restricted space.
“Conor’s death was a tragedy. He need not have been in the engine room at the time. When the worst happened, they couldn’t get him out in time to save him.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE senior enforcement lawyer Jon Mack and paralegal officer Mike Millman.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences can be found here.

items.title: Media company fined and director sentenced after employee suffers life-changing injuries after filming inside a moving vehicle
items.summary: Company fined £45000 Injured person has been unable to return to work No risk assessment had been carried out for the filming activity A media company has been fined and its director given a suspended custodial sentence after an employee suffered life-changing head and brain injuries when he fell from the back of a moving […]
items.body:
- Company fined £45000
- Injured person has been unable to return to work
- No risk assessment had been carried out for the filming activity
A media company has been fined and its director given a suspended custodial sentence after an employee suffered life-changing head and brain injuries when he fell from the back of a moving vehicle during filming in Devon .
The employee was working for Superhub Ltd on 14 May 2021 and was filming a video review of a new electric motorbike at Broadsands car park in Paignton.
After completing the planned filming using a drone, the decision was made to capture additional footage from a moving vehicle, with the motorbike following behind.
The employee climbed into the boot of a car driven by Superhub Ltd director James Foster, and they completed several laps of the car park. As the car began to move the boot liner slipped, causing the employee to fall onto the tarmac.
He sustained serious head and brain injuries requiring long-term care and has been unable to return to work since.
A joint investigation by Devon and Cornwall Police and the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that no risk assessment had been carried out for the filming activity. Investigators also found that the car was unsuitable for the task, as there was no provision to secure the employee or his filming equipment safely while the vehicle was moving.
HSE guidance states that camera operators should not film from footwells, sunroofs, open boots or side doors while a vehicle is moving unless suitable controls are in place to reduce the risk of injury or falling from the vehicle.
The guidance also states that tracking shots involving moving vehicles should only be carried out using suitable vehicles that maintain their structural integrity, with all crew members appropriately restrained.
Superhub Ltd, of Business Hub, Marine Parade, Paignton, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. Director James Foster pleaded guilty to breaching Section 37(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and to causing injury by wanton and furious driving.
Superhub Ltd was fined £45,000 and ordered to pay £3000 in costs. The Judge combined the individual charges and James Foster was sentenced to 16 months imprisonment suspended for 2 years. He was also ordered to pay £2500 in costs at Exeter Crown Court on Wednesday 14 October.
HSE Inspector Emma O’Hara said:
“An employee suffered life-changing injuries as a result of an incident that should never have happened and could easily have been prevented.
“Those responsible for filming activities must properly assess the risks and ensure that suitable equipment and safety measures are in place before work begins. No film, photo, or piece of content is ever worth risking someone’s life. Safety must always come first, and no filming activity should put people in harm’s way.”
“The sentences imposed today should serve as a reminder that HSE will not hesitate to take action against companies and individuals who fail to meet their responsibilities to protect people from harm.”
